key_points: Depois do jantar em Santa Theresa, Palha e Sophia ficam a sós e conversam sobre a noite.
Sophia conta ao marido que Rubião lhe fez uma declaração de amor.
Palha empalidece, e Sophia diz que é preciso fechar a porta a Rubião, de uma vez ou aos poucos.
Palha minimiza o caso como ingenuidade de Rubião, embora se mortifique com a ideia de que ele segurou as mãos da mulher.
Palha culpa Sophia por ter ido ao jardim, e ela responde que ele mesmo mandava tratar Rubião com atenções.
Palha atribui o episódio aos vinhos e não aceita romper com Rubião, um amigo a quem deve obrigações.
Sophia diz que presentes e joias não justificam o que Rubião fez, e Palha o chama de simplório.
Palha propõe escrever a Rubião para que não volte, e Sophia recua: basta cortar as relações aos poucos.
Palha confessa que deve muito dinheiro a Rubião, e Sophia concorda em apenas tratá-lo com mais frieza.
A conversa termina com Palha culpando as perdas do negócio, e Sophia vai deitar-se com dor de cabeça.
Maria Benedicta gostava de Carlos Maria e, quando Sophia prometeu arranjar-lhe um noivo, supôs que fosse ele, mas nada confessou.
Na comissão para a epidemia das Alagoas, Maria Benedicta conquista a estima de D. Fernanda, prima de Carlos Maria.
D. Fernanda tenta casar o primo com outra moça, Sonora, mas Carlos Maria esquiva-se e defende o celibato.
Carlos Maria prefere a conversação das mulheres à dos homens, que acha grosseiros e cansativos.
D. Fernanda, que simpatiza com os tristes, torna-se íntima de Maria Benedicta, mas a moça guarda o seu segredo.
D. Fernanda decide que o melhor é casar Maria Benedicta com Carlos Maria.
Pressionada por D. Fernanda, Maria Benedicta confessa, sem dizer o nome, uma paixão não correspondida.
D. Fernanda aconselha-a a deixar de poesia e casar, com esse homem ou com outro.
Maria Benedicta recusa-se a casar com outro e diz gostar dele como de Deus; D. Fernanda responde que um marido, mesmo mau, vale mais que um sonho.

Fruitful functions return a value: a return statement with an expression means return immediately and use that expression as the return value, in contrast to the void functions written so far, whose return value is None.

A function can have several return statements, for example one in each branch of a conditional, but it terminates as soon as one runs, and code the flow of execution can never reach, such as code after a return statement, is dead code.
Every possible path through a fruitful function should hit a return statement, because a function that reaches its end without one returns None, as the flawed absolute_value does when x is 0.
Incremental development avoids long debugging sessions by adding and testing only a small amount of code at a time, as shown by growing the distance function from an outline that just returns 0.0.

The key practices of incremental development are starting from a working program, using variables to hold intermediate values that can be displayed and checked, and treating print statements as scaffolding that helps build the program but is not part of the final product.
Functions can be composed: circle_area calls distance and area, first through temporary variables and then more concisely by composing the calls.

Boolean functions return True or False, hide complicated tests inside functions, usually have names that sound like yes/no questions such as is_divisible, and can return the result of a comparison directly and be used directly in conditionals.

The subset of Python covered so far is already a complete programming language in which anything that can be computed can be expressed, a claim first proved by Alan Turing and known as the Turing Thesis.
A recursive definition such as factorial translates directly into Python with a base case and a recursive call, and a stack diagram shows the return values being passed back up the stack.

The leap of faith is the alternative to following the flow of execution: you assume that a function call, including a recursive call, works correctly and returns the right result; for fibonacci, where following the flow of execution quickly becomes overwhelming, it makes clear that adding the two recursive results gives the right answer.

Calling factorial with 1.5 misses the base case and recurses forever, so the function checks its argument with isinstance and rejects non-integers and negative integers, a guardian pattern that makes it possible to prove the recursion terminates.

For debugging, functions create natural checkpoints: a failure comes from the arguments (a violated precondition), from the function itself (a violated postcondition), or from how the return value is used, and print statements at the start and end of a function make the flow of execution visible.

Inheritance is the ability to define a new class that is a modified version of an existing class, and the chapter demonstrates it with classes that represent playing cards, decks of cards and poker hands.

Card objects store suit and rank as integer codes, an encoding that maps suits and ranks to numbers so that cards are easy to compare, and the mapping is part of the program design rather than explicit code.

Class attributes such as suit_names and rank_names are defined inside a class but outside any method and are associated with the class object, unlike instance attributes such as suit and rank, which are associated with a particular instance; both are accessed with dot notation.

Programmer-defined types can override relational operators by providing __lt__, and comparing cards requires an arbitrary decision that suit is more important than rank, which tuple comparison can express concisely.

A Deck contains a list of cards as an attribute: its init method populates the 52 cards with a nested loop, and its __str__ method builds a list of strings and calls join, an efficient way to accumulate a large string.
Deck methods such as pop_card, add_card and shuffle wrap existing list and random module operations, and a method like add_card that uses another method without doing much work is called a veneer.

Hand inherits from Deck, making Deck the parent and Hand the child: Hand reuses methods such as pop_card and add_card but overrides __init__ so that a hand starts with an empty list of cards, and move_cards deals cards from one collection to another.

Inheritance can make programs more elegant, facilitate code reuse and reflect the natural structure of a problem, but it can also make programs difficult to read because a method's definition may be hard to find, and many things it does can be done as well or better without it.

Class diagrams are a more abstract representation than stack and object diagrams: they show classes and the relationships between them, namely HAS-A, IS-A and dependency, with multiplicity indicating how many references there are.

Inheritance can make debugging difficult because it may be hard to tell which method gets invoked; print statements can trace the flow of execution, and find_defining_class uses the mro method (method resolution order) to find the class that defines a method.

When you override a method, its interface should stay the same as the old one, with the same parameters, return type, preconditions and postconditions, so that functions written for a parent class also work with child classes; this rule is the Liskov substitution principle.

Data encapsulation is a development plan for discovering class interfaces: start with functions that use global variables, as the Markov code does, then encapsulate related variables as attributes of an object and transform the functions into methods, a refactoring that changes the design without changing the behavior.

chapter: CHAPTER II. OF THE LIBERTY OF THOUGHT AND DISCUSSION.
key_points: Even a government fully at one with the people has no right to coerce opinion: silencing one dissenter is as unjustified as his silencing mankind, because suppression robs the human race, including posterity and those who dissent from the opinion.
The suppressed opinion may be true, so all silencing of discussion assumes infallibility, and ages are no more infallible than individuals.

Acting on an opinion differs from forbidding its refutation: complete liberty to contradict an opinion is the very condition that justifies assuming its truth for action, because human judgment is valuable only in being correctable through discussion and experience.

Defending a restriction by a belief's usefulness rather than its truth does not help, because the usefulness of an opinion is itself a matter of opinion and the assumption of infallibility is merely shifted.
History shows the best men and doctrines condemned by sincere people: Socrates and Jesus were put to death as impious or blasphemous, and even Marcus Aurelius persecuted Christianity.

The saying that truth always triumphs over persecution is false: persecution has often succeeded, and truth's real advantage is only that it can be rediscovered in later ages until it escapes suppression.
In England legal penalties for opinion still exist, but the effective force is social stigma, which leads people to conceal their opinions.

This reticence sacrifices the moral courage of the human mind and cramps the minds of those who are not heretics, and an intellectually active people cannot arise where the great questions are closed to discussion.

Even a true opinion, if not fully and frequently discussed, becomes a dead dogma rather than a living truth, and anyone who knows only his own side of a case, without hearing the opposing arguments in their strongest form, knows little of it.

Without discussion the meaning of a doctrine is itself lost: creeds lose their vitality once they are inherited and no longer contested, as Christians profess the maxims of the New Testament without letting them guide their conduct.

Conflicting doctrines often share the truth: prevailing opinions are usually only part of it and dissenting ones supply the remainder, which holds even of Christian morality, which Mill calls incomplete and one-sided.

Demands that discussion stay temperate cannot be enforced, since the bounds cannot be fixed and law has no business restraining either side; the real morality of public discussion is to condemn unfairness on whichever side and to honour those who state opposing views honestly.

The chapter gives specimens of applying two maxims: the individual is not accountable to society for actions concerning only himself, but is accountable, and may be punished socially or legally, for actions prejudicial to others.
Harm to others does not always justify interference: those who lose out in legitimate competition have no right to immunity, and society intervenes only against fraud, treachery or force.

Free Trade rests on different grounds from individual liberty: trade is a social act and restrictions on it are wrong because they fail to produce the intended results, whereas measures meant to make a commodity hard to obtain, like the Maine Law, infringe the liberty of the buyer.

Preventing crime and accidents can justify some precautions, but where there is only a risk of harm a person should be warned rather than forcibly stopped, so poisons may be labelled and their sale recorded rather than prohibited.

Conduct normally self-regarding can be restricted when it harms others or breaches a duty to them: a person convicted of violence under the influence of drink may be placed under special restriction, and idleness may be punished in a man who fails to support his children.

People may advise whatever others are free to do, but it is doubtful whether those who profit from instigating it, like a gambling-house keeper or a pimp, should be free to do so, and Mill sets out the arguments on both sides without deciding whether to punish them.

Taxing stimulants merely to make them harder to get differs only in degree from prohibition, though taxing them for revenue is approved, and limiting the number of drink-houses to reduce temptation treats the labouring classes as children.

Engagements should generally be kept, but a contract to sell oneself as a slave is void because the principle of freedom cannot require that a person be free not to be free, and engagements such as marriage create obligations to those who rely on them and to third parties such as children.

Liberty is misapplied when it protects a parent's power over his children: the State should require every child's education while generally leaving its provision to others, because a general State education moulds people to be alike.
Bringing a child into existence without a fair prospect of providing for it is a moral crime, so laws forbidding marriage to those who cannot support a family do not violate liberty.

Even government action that restricts no one's liberty is open to three objections: individuals may do the thing better, doing it themselves educates them, and adding unnecessarily to the government's power is a great evil.

Absorbing a country's ability into a bureaucracy enslaves governors and governed alike, so the guiding rule is the greatest dissemination of power consistent with efficiency with the greatest centralisation of information, because the worth of a State is the worth of the individuals composing it.
